# Implementation notes

Source: https://github.com/wrnrlr/goal-mirror/blob/master/docs/implementation.md

*Last updated: 2025-02-16*

# Implementation notes

This document talks about Goal's implementation. It's intended to be a kind of
starting point before digging into the code or extending it, while telling as
well how some things ended up in a way or another. The document is
*occasionally* updated, but it was originally written in a blog post kind of
style, so it's not a very concise introduction.

# Choosing the implementation language

Among suitable languages, I chose Go because I know it very well and feel
comfortable with it. It might not be the usual go-to language for implementing
interpreters, but it has quite a few good points for such task:

* A comprehensive standard library, without requiring more external
  dependencies.
* Higher-level language for embedding than what C provides, so that it's easier
  to extend.
* Low-level enough that things go fast.
* Fast compilation.

OCaml is a language I know that mostly fits too, except for the first point.
Of course, given current trends, I did think of languages like Zig (built-in
SIMD) and Rust (with it's excellent regexp library), but I only know the first
on the surface, I don't feel comfortable with the second, and SIMD comes at
quite a cost in code complexity and portability anyway. *Update: Goal has now
assembly SIMD implementations of various algorithms for amd64*.

Also, Go gives us good garbage collection out of the box, which is quite a good
thing, as my knowledge about garbage collection implementation is limited.  I
know there are GC libraries for most non-GC languages, but it's still one less
thing to worry about. As a tradeoff, we cannot catch out of memory errors
reliably in programs.

Even counting the recent generics addition, a downside of Go for implementing
an array language interpreter is the lack of macros. However, code generation
helps, and given Goal's somewhat minimalist design, it's manageable and not an
issue for me.

Interestingly, while Go and Goal are quite the opposite in terms of conciseness
due to the gap between scalar and array paradigms, they both encourage idioms
over abstraction, and writing executable code over writing types: this might
explain why this is at least the third project for an array language in Go.

# Context

The `Context` struct type in `context.go` represents the state of the
interpreter.  It's the first type that you will encounter if you want to embed
Goal in a program. The `Context` type records all the information needed for
execution, including arrays of constants, globals, lambdas, extra built-ins, or
error locations, so it's the natural entry point for embedded usage. From an
internals perspective, there's nothing unusual there, so we'll rather talk
about program representation next.

# Program representation

The compiler chain is quite typical: scanning goes first (`scan/scanner.go`),
then we parse into an AST (`parser.go` and `ast.go`), which is then compiled
into bytecode (`compiler.go`), and then finally run by a VM (`vm.go`).

One thing to note is that, in Goal, variables are resolved during compilation
but still textual in the AST. The compiler is mainly one-pass, except for
lambdas, which have a variable resolution pass followed by a fast simple
variable liveness analysis that works well for typical array code with limited
branching and is used to conservatively reuse dead immutable arrays. A very
basic constant-folding pass is done too; it also detects statically tail
calls performed with the special self-referencing `o` variable.

Our “bytecode” opcodes are actually of type `int32` (see `opcodes.go`). This
design is originally inspired from how it's done in
[GoAWK](https://benhoyt.com/writings/goawk/). Though values in GoAWK are a bit
different, they are the same size as Goal's (four words), so stack-handling in
both is quite close.

# Value representation

Go's interface types are a quite good fit for representing the various kinds of
values in a dynamic language like Goal. Most interpreters written in Go have a
`value.go` file where a `Value` interface type is defined. This Value interface
is satisfied by all kinds of values supported by the language (of course
sometimes it's called differently, like Object or whatever :-). Having values
as an interface, as opposed to, say, a sum-type or an union-type in other
languages, has the advantage of allowing easy extensibility, as adding new
kinds of native values just means implementing an interface for a new type.

Goal's value representation is a bit more complicated than usual: the expected
Value interface is called `BV` and is satisfied by all *boxed* values, but
values themselves are represented by a struct type called `V`.

``` go
// V contains a boxed or unboxed value.
type V struct {
	kind valueKind // valInt, valFloat, valBoxed, ...
	uv   int64     // unboxed integer or float value
	bv   BV        // boxed value
}

// BV is the interface satisfied by all boxed values. It can be satisfied
// by user-defined types.
//
// Ordered boxed values can also satisfy the [OrderedBV] interface, so that
// they are supported by sort and bins.
//
// Types that are not comparable or ordered in a meaningful way may implement
// Append with nil Context without fully respecting the unique hash
// requirements: the only consequence is that search and self-search primitives
// will produce unspecified results when working on such values.
type BV interface {
	// Append appends a unique program representation of the value to dst,
	// and returns the extended buffer. It should not store the returned
	// buffer elsewhere, so that it's possible to safely convert it to
	// string without allocations. The compact boolean determines whether
	// insignificant whitespace should be removed or not. If passed a nil
	// context, Append should produce a unique string suitable for hashing.
	Append(ctx *Context, dst []byte, compact bool) []byte
	// Matches reports whether the two values match like in x~y.
	Matches(BV) bool
	// Type returns the name of the value's type. It may be used to compare
	// unordered values using lexicographic order.  This means Type should
	// return different values for non-comparable values.
	Type() string
}
```

Hence, Goal has unboxed integer and floating point values (by interpreting the
`uv` field as one type or the other depending on the kind field), as well as
unboxed types for built-in functions and lambdas. This makes scalar code faster
and more memory-friendly by keeping numeric atoms in the stack.  Although the
`V` struct is less compact than a union struct in C (we need four words), it
does perform quite well in practice, as Go is good at efficiently copying small
types up to a few words.

# Primitives

There's nothing really surprising in the way primitives are implemented: they
are represented by the `VariadicFunc` type as follows:

``` go
// VariadicFunc represents a variadic function. The slice of arguments is in
// stack order: the first argument is the last element.
//
// Most Context methods are available for use in variadic functions, except the
// ones that could affect the current execution state (Compile, Run).
//
// See RegisterMonad and RegisterDyad for defining new variadic builtins usable
// from Goal.
type VariadicFunc func(*Context, []V) V
```

In other words, they take an execution context and a list of arguments, and
they return a new value. Each variadic function inspects dynamically its
arguments and is usually polysemic depending on types. One gotcha, though:
arguments are in reverse order, because the slice comes from the VM's stack.

Array languages face a major difficulty with primitives in that most of them
have to handle various different specialized array types, mostly for
performance reasons.

For example, there's a type for arrays of bytes `AB`, another for arrays of
64-bit integers `AI`, and another for arrays of 64-bit floats `AF`.  Goal's
user does not have to think much about this, and can treat booleans as 0 and 1
without worrying about whether they're stored compactly as a byte or an int64.
One can also use 4.0 as an integer (but not 4.5), and generally perform most
operations on numeric types without doing any explicit conversions between
floating point and integer.  The implementation, though, must handle each case
for each operand, which can quickly become daunting. And there's no really any
way, except for heavy macro usage, to avoid handling all the cases: generics
can help to abstract some algorithms, but they don't help much to deal with
many type combinations simultaneously. Also, specific types have often better
algorithms than a generic one (for example sort and search for arrays of
byte-sized integers).

For simple unary functions, a variadic function looks like this:

``` go
// vfSubtract implements the - variadic verb.
func vfSubtract(_ *Context, args []V) V {
	switch len(args) {
	case 1:
		return negate(args[0])
	case 2:
		return subtract(args[1], args[0])
	default:
		return extArith(subtract, args)
	}
}

// negate returns -x.
func negate(x V) V {
	if x.IsI() {
		return NewI(-x.I())
	}
	if x.IsF() {
		return NewF(-x.F())
	}
	switch xv := x.bv.(type) {
	case S:
		return NewS(strings.TrimRightFunc(string(xv), unicode.IsSpace))
	case *AB:
		r := makeNoZeroI(xv.Len())
		for i, xi := range xv.Slice {
			r[i] = -int64(xi)
		}
		return NewAI(r)
	case *AI:
		r := xv.reuse()
		vec.SubiI(r.Slice, 0, xv.Slice)
		return NewV(r)
	case *AF:
		r := xv.reuse()
		vec.SubfF(r.Slice, 0, xv.Slice)
		return NewV(r)
	case *AS:
		r := xv.reuse()
		for i, xi := range xv.Slice {
			r.Slice[i] = strings.TrimRightFunc(xi, unicode.IsSpace)
		}
		return NewV(r)
	case *AV:
		return mapAV(xv, negate)
	case *D:
		return newDictValues(xv.keys, negate(NewV(xv.values)))
	default:
		return panicType("-x", "x", x)
	}
}
```

The binary case is more intricate, as the number of cases to handle becomes
quadratic in the number of types (among those that can be combined).

Most of the function is quite self-explanatory, except for the `.reuse` method,
which is an internal optimization that returns an array value of same-length
and type which may reuse the original's value intact memory, if it's deemed
reusable by the reference count system for array values. Also, the `mapAV`
function is used for the generic array case `AV`, which is handled recursively
in the same way for many monadic primitives.

If performance is not a concern, like for example for the APL-like bignum
calculator [ivy](https://pkg.go.dev/robpike.io/ivy) (also written in Go!), it's
possible to handle this more simply: all arrays are there slices of type
`[]Value` where `Value` is an interface, and operations are not vectorized for
specific types, so array operations are deduced easily from operations on
atoms.

In our case, some things were even a bit more verbose than they would have been
in C, because in Go type conversions have to be explicit all the time, and
there are no macros, meaning more code duplication for the various numeric
types. For the extreme case of dyadic arithmetic primitives, I originally used
some code generation (written in Goal). This is similar to how they're usually
implemented in C array language interpreters by using macros. *Update: I
manually rewrote that code since then, as it wasn't that much work relative to
the whole project and, in many cases, specific optimizations can be made, so a
manual approach is simpler to maintain despite being more verbose. The result
is in `arithd.go`.*

Other than that, some array primitives do require some algorithmic work, in
particular self-search functions, though there's no way I'm going to explain
this better than [BQN implementation
notes](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/implementation/), so there you go. I did
not optimize as far as BQN, but I picked a few ideas from there.

# Performance

*Update: [see
FAQ](https://anaseto.codeberg.page/goal-docs/chap-FAQ.html#performance) for
more up-to-date, concise and practical information about performance.*

I talked about scalar performance above but did not give any numbers. There's
some benchmarks you can run with `go test -bench .`, and see how they perform
on your system, which is probably faster than my cheap computer. *Update: the
`internal/vec` sub-package has also micro-benchmarks for amd64 SIMD algorithms.*

For an array language, there are two kinds of perspectives on performance:
*scalar performance* and *array performance*.

I'm not sure micro-benchmarks for scalar code are that meaningful, as they
change a lot from one system to another and are not representative of real
world applications. That said, to give an order of magnitude, on my OpenBSD
machine, things like the naive fibonacci (fib 35) function completed faster
than Perl, more or less like Python, though I'm not going to celebrate because
on a Linux machine Python ran more than twice as fast for this same
micro-benchmark (but Perl ran like Goal).

Whatever, I would say that Goal's *scalar performance* is decent. Quite a few
array programming languages (like J) have done well without that, because
what's more likely to matter in practice is *array performance*. You're indeed
normally going to be using whole-array primitives on performance sensitive
parts with large arrays, so it's going to go fast, at least fast like in
typical Go code *(Update: often quite faster than pure Go code now on amd64 due
to assembly SIMD implementations of many operations)*.

In my experience, performance was usually comparable to ngn/k's for small
practical problems (like AoC), with main differences being due to array
representation. Goal represents all arrays as slices, so there is an overhead
when allocating many small arrays; also, ngn/k has specialized array types for
int16 and int32 integers, so some algorithms using large arrays of medium-range
integers can be faster and use less memory.  On the flip side, using slices
improves worst case complexity of some uses of structural primitives, as well
as performance of some string-handling functionality like trim or split, the
latter being further improved thanks to having a dedicated list of strings
type.

Also, talking about performance, the refcount system that allows for memory
reuse in many builtins (like amortized constant time append) has been maybe the
major source of bugs during development: I know what people mean now when they
say refcounting stuff is hard! Thankfully, because memory management is done by
Go's GC, I ended up with a simplified but good-enough lightweight
implementation of refcounting that was much easier to get correct, because it
is limited to non-nested arrays (nested values are always marked as
definitively immutable).

---

# Problems

Source: https://github.com/wrnrlr/goal-mirror/blob/master/docs/problems.md

*Last updated: 2024-10-13*

# Problems

This file contains some design notes about (mostly minor) tradeoffs and
limitations in the language that either aren't still covered in the FAQ, or
don't really have a place there. Items are roughly sorted in decreasing order
of (subjectively) perceived practical importance.

## empty generic arrays

Empty generic arrays lose element type information, defaulting to an empty list
of list of strings for fill-related matters. Smarter prototypes/fills could
solve this partially, but Goal's behavior is simpler to understand and
implement.

## keyword verbs and variables share the same namespace

This means it's not possible to add new keywords in the core in a
backwards-compatible way without risking naming conflicts with user code.

It's not really an issue as long as any new keywords are added in extensions,
preferably with an optional configurable dot prefix, or if they're added within
a reserved prefix like `rt.`.  Other possible interesting default prefixes for
future core extensions could be `map.` (for a mutable hash table), `heap.`,
`http.`, but those would not be built by default in Goal, as they're not as
universally useful as `os` in typical scripting, so they would not really
qualify as “reserved”.

Note that many programming languages rich in keywords have this kind of issue,
like AWK or Perl. The latter solves those in flexible, but complicated, ways
(like making explicit a version `use v5.32`), while AWK simply solves it by
being minimalistic and stable. In the case of Goal, I don't think a complicated
solution is needed either: sharing AWK's and K's minimalistic design, the base
language is mostly complete, so there should not be a need to add any new
built-in keywords without a dot prefix (I at least don't have any plans of
adding any).

The only question could be additions in the only built-in extension `os`,
that's imported without prefix, but new additions would correspond to more
uncommon functionality, so they could just use an `os.` prefix, or be done in a
different way (like using filehandles being callable and take advantage of
`h..field` syntax for providing a method-like API).

## eval same location with different prefix

When using eval with a same location, but a different prefix, the source is
compiled and run again. This might not always be the desired behavior, but
given Goal's namespacing semantics, it's not clear how we could do better.

## namespaces are not first-class values

Namespacing is flat, with some niceties for working with dot prefixes.
Dictionaries and field expressions can mostly replace the need for dynamic
namespaces, but not as well as a dedicated solution would. The simplicity
benefits of the current system are worth it, in my opinion.

## `csv` builtin fills missing columns

The `csv` builtin fills missing columns with empty strings. This is usually ok,
but it's not possible to distinguish missing fields from empty fields. Could be
solved in a backwards-compatible way by using left argument to provide an extra
option to work around this, though it's probably not worth it (at least for
now).

## colon as verb and syntax

The various meanings of `:` are easy to resolve for humans in practice, but
it's still a bit overloaded, and it's not clear all the cases are handled in
the most intuitive or useful way: for example `+:` can be both an assignment
operation or a monadic verb depending on how it's used. At least the
number of meanings decreased by one with the removal of digraph adverbs.

## find index

The `?` verb returns the index of the first occurrence, both for arrays and
strings. It's usually what you want, but not always. At least for strings,
having an all indices version could be useful (though rarely enough that a
user-code solution might be acceptable: most array languages share this
situation).

Also, find is rank-insensitive for arrays, which is less surprising and
simpler, but less useful than rank-sensitive versions when searching for a
single non-atomic value. However, since strings are atomic in Goal, we would
benefit less from rank-sensitivity than ngn/k.

## flip `+x`

On ragged arrays it cycles. It could pad with zeros instead and maybe that
would be more useful in some cases, but you usually expect replication in the
case of an atom, so unless we don't care about consistency here, we can't have
both.

Also, like in other K dialects, and unlike APL derivatives with true
multi-dimensional arrays, flip can be slow if nested arrays are short.

## trim spaces

There is `""^s` and `-s`, but no builtin to trim spaces only at beginning of
string without regexps.

## pad fields `i!s` uses number of code points for width

It does not handle wide-characters. Go's standard library doesn't provide a
`wcwidth` function, and we don't want to require external libraries. We could
reimplement that, but given that format strings `s$` also use number of code
points for width, it's more consistent to keep things as-is. Current behavior
is also easier to implement efficiently and should be enough for most common
practical usages.

## bins is inconsistent with find

This is inherited from BQN, as we used the same convention for bins. There are
benefits to start from zero, in particular in Goal, since negative numbers
force bigger integer size for arrays (we only have uint8 and int64 arrays).

## no splice function

It's mostly used for text-processing in K, which in Goal is done in another
way. It remains true that there's no really efficient way to delete or insert
items in the middle of an array (concatenating slices forces a new copy even
though we could have reused the original in some cases). I haven't come accross
any problematic examples in practice.

## no inverse function

We cannot use the `symbol?` approach used in ngn/k for inverses, as `s?`
already has a meaning in goal, so such cases are handled individually.

For example, the `csv` builtin, `"c"$` and `"b"$` simply work both ways in a
idempotent way. This is usually what we want unless there are mixed type
inputs, which should not happen in practice in such cases.

Not all cases work like those, though: the `json` builtin does parsing in the
monadic case and encoding in the dyadic case.

All in all, I'm not convinced by inverse functions, as often the functions are
not bijections (for example `&I` vs `=I`), so there's some extra considerations
to learn for each case anyway.  Also, in some cases, one of the directions
might benefit from extra arguments (like the `json` builtin) that don't make
sense for the inverse.

## no deep-where `&x`

Because we use `&` pervasively for strings, we cannot have deep-where
because of its dependency on both rank (which we don't do for find either) and
type. I'm not sure what an efficient implementation of deep-where would be,
either.

## no title-case function

We could maybe use `round` for this, as related functions `_` and `uc` do
lower-case and upper-case already. It would still be not very intuitive, and
title-case is not very common, so an extension with more advanced utf8 and
unicode stuff seems a more appropriate place for it.

## rt.ofs is not idiomatic (solved: removed feature)

It's mostly there due to AWK/Perl influence, but is quite useless in practice,
as join `s/` avoids the need for it, and using it for special behavior in array
interpolation to avoid doing an explicit join outside is probably more
error-prone than useful.

The only use for it is avoiding concatenation of a long list of large strings
that need to be output, for reducing memory usage, but Goal is unlikely to be
used in a setting where avoiding that concatenation matters, as the whole
language is thought mainly for applications where there's enough memory to keep
all the data you're working with, and it's possible anyway to divide such a
long list in smaller parts and process them separately.

This problem could actually be solved simply by removing it, as I'm not sure
anyone ever used that feature anyway.

---
